extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of religion / comparative religion
extracted.subtask_description: Expository/philosophical essay analyzing Christianity’s ethical spirit (asceticism, celibacy), its relation to other religions (Brahmanism, Buddhism, Judaism), and mechanisms of religious transmission and conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of spirit/ethical tendency over myth
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit and ethical tendency are what is essential in a religion, not the myths in which these are clothed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a religion, focus on its core ethical/spiritual principles (e.g., denial of the will, boundless love) rather than on its particular mythological forms; myths serve as 'vehicles' to make abstract truths accessible to the masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism (denial of the will) as the kernel of Christianity
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity’s inmost kernel consists in the denial of one’s self and the overcoming of the world (asceticism), which is fundamentally opposed to optimism and natural affirmation of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a Christian practice or doctrine preserves the ascetic principle (e.g., valorization of celibacy, self-denial); loss of asceticism (as argued for parts of Protestantism) implies departure from authentic Christianity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage as a concession; celibacy as higher consecration
rubrics_metrics.description: In genuine Christianity marriage is 'merely a compromise with the sinful nature of man' allowed for the weak; celibacy and virginity are set up as the higher consecration through which one enters the ranks of the elect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Christian moral systems by how they rank marriage versus continence; historical testimony (Fathers, Councils, sects like the Shakers/Trappists) is used to support celibacy’s privileged status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious transmission requires mythical vehicles for the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The great abstract truth (e.g., need of deliverance, denial of the will) must borrow a 'mythical vehicle' to be practically accessible to the majority of mankind, who cannot grasp abstract philosophical truth directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a religion’s forms, understand myths and rites as necessary pedagogical tools for conveying difficult truths to the general populace; philosophy presents the content 'pure and unmixed' for the few capable of abstract thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment of authenticity by ethical orientation (pessimism vs optimism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity is characterized by a pessimistic view of the world (world as realm of suffering, lorded by the devil) and the need for deliverance; Judaism (and some pagan traditions) are optimistic and thus differ essentially from Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and compare religions by their fundamental ethical outlook (optimistic acceptance of the world vs pessimistic denial/renunciation); this determines perceived authenticity of a religion’s core message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional response to doctrinal consistency that threatens policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups (e.g., Tatianites, Encratites) that consistently teach perfect continence were declared heretical by the Church, not necessarily for incoherence but because their doctrine ran counter to the Church’s practical policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating what counts as 'heresy' historically, consider institutional interests and policy (ability of a religion to function in the world) as decisive factors beyond mere doctrinal truth or logical consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monasticism as methodical denial of the will; measure by depth and sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Monasticism is 'that methodical denial of the will practised in common' whose moral worth depends on the profundity of renunciation and exclusion of secondary ends; its perfection is shown by strictness and exclusion of ulterior motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monastic or communal religious orders by sincerity and severity of renunciation (e.g., La Trappe’s severity), whether practices genuinely exclude worldly ends or have been corrupted by secondary aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion through immediate, intense suffering as evidence of genuine renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Profound internal transformation (denial of the will) frequently occurs after deeply felt personal suffering (e.g., tragic events, confronting death), leading to authentic renunciation and religious conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider biographical accounts of conversion (e.g., Abbé Rancé, last words of condemned criminals) as evidence that intense suffering can precipitate genuine moral/spiritual change; such cases serve as psychological support for theories of conversion by suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy’s role: present truth 'sensu proprio' for the few
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should present religious truths in abstract, unmixed form (sensu proprio) for those capable of thinking, while religions provide allegorical forms for the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate criteria for success: philosophy succeeds if it conveys the pure abstract content to thinkers; a religion succeeds if it can enshrine the same truth in accessible, durable mythic forms.
